## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

**Outcome:** The drop-ins are valid and take effect on OpenSSH 10.5p1. Three issues were found. The reload guard stops non-chroot installs when sshd is not running. The pinned key exchange lists remove OpenSSH's default post-quantum key exchange. The client `HostKeyAlgorithms` list breaks connections to already-trusted hosts.

**Verified:** Both files are written with the intended content and modes (sshd 0600, client 0644). `sshd -t`, `sshd -T` and `ssh -G` accept them on OpenSSH 10.5p1. Every directive takes effect because Arch's packaged `sshd_config` and `ssh_config` include the `.d` directories at the top, and a baseline/PR `sshd -T` comparison shows each value changed as written. When sshd is active, the script validates and then reloads. ISO installs under `arch-chroot` skip the reload block, because `arch-chroot` sets `SYSTEMD_IN_CHROOT=1` and systemctl then prints no unit state.

### Reload guard matches `inactive` and stops non-chroot installs

`systemctl is-active sshd | grep -q active` is a substring match, so it also matches `inactive`. openssh is always installed on Omarchy (pulled in through gnome-keyring's gcr dependencies), but sshd is not enabled, so on a booted system the state is `inactive` and the branch runs:

| sshd state | Host keys | Branch | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `inactive` | none (Arch creates them on first sshd start) | runs | `sshd -t` exits 1: `sshd: no hostkeys available -- exiting.` |
| `inactive` | present | runs | `systemctl reload` fails: `sshd.service is not active, cannot reload.` |
| `active` | present | runs | validates and reloads |
| `failed`, or under `arch-chroot` | n/a | skipped | continues |

`run_logged` returns that status to `install.sh`, which runs under `set -e` with an ERR trap, so the installer stops. This table comes from a sandboxed run of the PR head's `run_logged` flow with `systemctl` results stubbed from systemd source, plus a real `sshd -t` without host keys. No full `boot.sh` install was run in a VM.

**Impact:** The online/manual install path (`boot.sh` on an existing Arch system) stops at this step. ISO installs are not affected.

**Suggested change:** Use the exit status instead of the text, as `migrations/1751134568.sh` already does:

```bash
if systemctl is-active --quiet sshd; then
  sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
fi
```

### Pinned `KexAlgorithms` removes the default post-quantum key exchange

OpenSSH 10.x prefers `mlkem768x25519-sha256`, followed by the `sntrup761x25519` hybrids. The PR replaces both the server and client lists with `curve25519-sha256`, `curve25519-sha256@libssh.org` and two finite-field DH groups, so no post-quantum hybrid remains. Loopback results from sandboxed OpenSSH 10.5p1 with private configs and synthetic keys:

| Client → server | Negotiated KEX | Non-PQ warning |
|---|---|---|
| default → default | `mlkem768x25519-sha256` | no |
| PR client → default | `curve25519-sha256` | no (suppressed) |
| default → PR sshd | `curve25519-sha256` | yes, on every connection |

The client warning is suppressed because OpenSSH prints it only when `KexAlgorithms` is not set explicitly (`sshconnect.c`, `readconf.c`). The PR's server list also re-adds finite-field DH groups, which sshd stopped offering by default in 10.0.

**Impact:** Every connection from or to an Omarchy machine with this drop-in falls back from post-quantum hybrid to classical key exchange. On the client side this happens silently. Modern clients connecting to the Omarchy sshd show the three-line `** WARNING: connection is not using a post-quantum key exchange algorithm.`

**Suggested change:** Leave `KexAlgorithms` at the OpenSSH default. If a specific algorithm needs to go, remove it with the `-` prefix syntax instead of replacing the list.

### Client `HostKeyAlgorithms` breaks already-trusted hosts, ECDSA-only servers and host certificates

An explicit `HostKeyAlgorithms` list turns off OpenSSH's ordering by known_hosts entries (`sshconnect2.c`). The client then picks Ed25519 whenever the server offers it. A known_hosts entry of a different type for the same host counts as a changed key (`hostfile.c`). Sandboxed loopback results:

| Server / known_hosts | Default client | PR client |
|---|---|---|
| Ed25519 + ECDSA + RSA keys, known_hosts has only ECDSA (or only RSA) | verifies, proceeds | `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!`, `Host key verification failed.` |
| ECDSA-only server | verifies, proceeds | `no matching host key type found` |
| Ed25519 host certificate, `@cert-authority` entry | verifies certificate | host key verification fails |

The changed-key failure also occurs with `StrictHostKeyChecking=ask`, because that setting only prompts for new hosts.

**Impact:** Users whose known_hosts already trusts a server's ECDSA or RSA key get a changed-host-key failure the next time they connect. ECDSA-only devices and certificate-based host trust stop working. User login keys are not affected.

**Suggested change:** Leave `HostKeyAlgorithms` at the default, or remove specific algorithms with the `-` prefix syntax.

**Narrower cipher and KEX lists:** In the sandboxed loopback runs, the PR client could not connect to a CTR-only server (`no matching cipher found`) or to a server offering only NIST ECDH and `diffie-hellman-group14-sha256` (`no matching key exchange method found`). The PR sshd rejected a client limited to the same NIST/group14 set. The `MACs` lines have no effect, because every allowed cipher is AEAD and OpenSSH skips MAC negotiation for AEAD ciphers (`kex.c`).

**Other sshd directives:** `PubkeyAuthentication yes` and `StrictModes yes` restate the defaults. `PasswordAuthentication` is left enabled. `MaxSessions 4` refuses a fifth concurrent session over one multiplexed connection.

**Existing installs:** The script runs only from `install/config/all.sh`, and the PR adds no migration, so existing installs do not get the drop-ins. If a migration is added, it needs the corrected guard, because a stopped sshd is the normal state on booted systems.

**Precedence and branch:** OpenSSH uses the first value it finds, so any drop-in that sorts before `99-omarchy-hardening.conf` (and any `~/.ssh/config` entry) overrides these settings. The repository's default branch `quattro` already has an opt-in `bin/omarchy-setup-security-sshd`. It writes `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-omarchy-hardening.conf` (password authentication off, only after a key is authorized) and checks the result with `sshd -t` and `sshd -T`. A `10-` file wins over this `99-` file for any shared keyword, which may matter when choosing the target branch and file name.

**Optional test improvement:** `test/ssh-hardening-test.sh` passes (8/8) even when `systemctl is-active` reports `inactive`, the state in which the installer stops, because the `sudo` stub makes `sshd -t` and `systemctl reload` always succeed. The unprefixed `systemctl is-active` call is also not stubbed, so the test queries the host's service manager. Stubbing `systemctl` in the test, covering `inactive`, `active` and `failed`, and letting the stubbed `sshd -t` and `reload` fail for an inactive unit would catch the guard bug.

---

## Review information

**Test scope:** Pinned head `07c77c03fc318e76dcf7bcbe6adbb6c600a69c84`, read against OpenSSH portable 10.5p1 source, Arch `openssh` 10.5p1 packaging, systemd v262 and arch-install-scripts v31. Runtime checks ran in a network-isolated sandbox: `bash -n` on both scripts, the PR test, `sshd -t`/`sshd -T`/`ssh -G` on private config copies, and loopback-only sshd/ssh connections using synthetic host keys and private known_hosts files. The installer flow was exercised with stubbed `systemctl` results. No full install or VM run was performed, and no connection was made to real servers or forges. The frequency of affected known_hosts histories and ECDSA-only or certificate-based servers was not measured.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis; independent Opus 5.5 Xhigh and GPT 6 Sol Xhigh technical assessments, with targeted follow-up questions to confirm claims resting on one assessment; Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.
